dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Read both fixture next-shims.d.ts files and enumerated every next/* module to shim; grounded the shim contract in actual type declarations rather than memory.

Consulted Vite plugin API types (vite/types/plugin.d.ts, dist/node/index.d.ts) and @vitejs/plugin-rsc internals (plugin-Xwi, plugin-BGm, types/index.d.ts) to understand the plugin lifecycle and RSC environment setup.

Studied fixture pages for real usage (getStaticProps/Paths, getServerSideProps, _app, _document, API routes, middleware) and read Next.js dist source for link/router/head/compat-router; noted RSC semantics like server actions and encryption keys (step 31/504).
Once shim/plugin coding began, reference consultation essentially ceased across ~150 debugging steps — no return to upstream source to resolve semantics; research was front-loaded, not sustained.
The single reference re-consult during the long debugging phase (checking vite package.json bin field), confirming research was not continuous throughout the build.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent performed systematic upfront reference mining — reading both fixture next-shims.d.ts, the Vite plugin API surface, and @vitejs/plugin-rsc internals, plus fixture pages and Next.js dist source — grounding each shim in an actual signature, which clears the level-5 anchor and reaches toward 8 (mapping vendored source to subsystems, extracting contracts from every fixture shim). However, it falls short of 8-10 because that research was heavily front-loaded and abandoned during the ~400-step debugging phase (only one re-consult at step 187), with no re-checking of source to resolve ambiguous routing/RSC/cache semantics as they surfaced. Solid grounding but not the sustained, self-correcting cross-referencing the top anchors describe, placing it at 6.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Agent lays out an explicit ordered build sequence (index/plugin -> cli -> shims -> ssr -> router) and enumerates the subsystems, showing subsystem identification and a rough order — but it is a file-creation order, not a dependency-aware verify-as-you-go plan, and carries no done-criteria per milestone.

Numbered requirement-mirroring list of everything the package must do, then it proceeds to build all subsystems (all shims + 734-line SSR renderer + router + CLI) before running any test — a big-bang build rather than a minimal end-to-end slice first.

Only after many 0/325 runs does it articulate the vertical-slice idea ('minimal vinext that just resolves next/* imports... then incrementally add features') — the right instinct, but it is never executed as a milestone plan; work collapses into infrastructure firefighting.
Late trajectory shows repeated root-cause guessing about why servers won't start with no milestone re-planning or interface management; the through-line is lost.
Final submissions summarize files built but never achieved an incrementally-verified subsystem baseline; done-criteria remained the whole suite, which never passed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified the major subsystems and chose a broadly sensible order (plugin/resolution before shims before SSR before router/CLI), which reaches toward anchor 5, but the 'order' was a file-writing sequence with no per-milestone done-criteria and no dependency-aware incremental verification. Rather than sequencing a minimal end-to-end path first (anchor 8), it built everything before testing and then spent the bulk of the run firefighting infrastructure; a belated recognition of the vertical-slice approach (steps 175-185) was never carried through. This places it above a flat bullet list (3) but short of the rough done-criteria and sensible verifiable ordering of a full 5, i.e. a 4.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Repeatedly runs the full run_tests.sh suite as a pass/fail oracle (tee to /tmp files, tail output); reads run_tests.py/utils.py to understand the health check. This is oracle-style use of the suite (anchor 3).
Uses node --check on dist/cli.js, index.js, ssr/render.js and loops over all shims to catch silent syntax errors — verification beyond 'it compiles' but confined to static checks.

Builds smaller probes: starts the CLI manually (timeout node dist/cli.js dev), curls localhost to confirm HTTP 200, then npm-packs and installs the tgz into a temp app to reproduce the exact test flow — root-cause diagnosis of 'FAILED to start' rather than pure pass/fail.

Manual end-to-end simulation of the harness (pack/install/npx vinext dev, check .bin symlink) to isolate why the server never launches. Good targeted probing, but never advances past server startup to any subsystem behavior.

Ends still at 0/325; dev never worked and build/start behavior was never verified functionally, and no fixture was ever stood up to observe SSR/SSG/actions — so subsystem-level verification (anchor 5) was never reached.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent goes beyond anchor 3's bare pass/fail oracle: it constructs smaller probes (manual CLI start + curl, node --check across files, npm-pack/install simulation) and interprets the 'FAILED to start' symptom by root cause. But it never reaches anchor 5: it runs no targeted test subsets or per-subsystem fixtures, never gets the dev/build/start paths actually working, and never stands up a fixture to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior — all verification stays pinned at the infrastructure 'server responds' layer. That places it between 3 and 5, at a 4.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Runs the suite and reports precise aggregate pass counts (0/325), re-running after config/package.json fixes to catch whether servers now start — tracks pass count and re-checks after changes (anchor 5).

Recognizes it is looping ('After 15+ test iterations, consistently 0/325') and steps back to a manual curl probe + npm-pack simulation instead of blindly retrying — a level-8 trait, but isolated and it never escaped 0.
Notices the suite now reports 0/335 and correctly reasons the CLI is never invoked (empty startup log); still only an aggregate number, no per-subsystem breakdown because nothing passes.

For ~290 steps the pass count is pinned at 0 while the agent restates many rotating root-cause hypotheses (bin symlink, ESM require, heredoc corruption, network) without convergence — coarse single-metric tracking, no by-area done-vs-remaining model, no regression detection possible.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently tracked an aggregate pass count and re-ran the suite after changes (anchor 5), and at points explicitly recognized it was looping and stepped back to manual probing (an anchor-8 flash). However, it never built a structured pass-rate-by-area / done-vs-remaining view, could not detect cross-subsystem regressions (it was pinned at 0 the entire back half), and largely restated the same aggregate conclusion with rotating hypotheses rather than converging. That lands it solidly at the level-5 anchor with only fleeting reach toward 8, not sustained.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: After discovering dev servers fail (0/325), the agent recognizes the CLI/plugin approach is wrong and pivots the whole server architecture to a raw Node HTTP server that bypasses Vite (step 208) — a foundational change, but one that hacks around the requirement rather than fixing Vite integration.

Repeatedly reverts to a 'dead-simple CLI' serving hardcoded HTML solely to pass health checks. This is patching around the flawed foundation rather than absorbing the cost of the correct design, and shows oscillation rather than convergence.

A genuine diagnosis-driven design revision: realizes a bare-specifier `vite` import cannot resolve from its own package directory and reworks the CLI to spawn the Vite binary from the fixture's node_modules. This is real architectural correction from a falsified assumption.

Explicitly names the problem — 'spending too much time on infrastructure' and 'CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL ISSUE: raw HTTP server' — showing awareness that the foundation is wrong, but the awareness never turns into a clean, sustained refactor.

Near the end it swings back to 'correct architecture' using dynamic import('vite')/createServer, then to an ultra-minimal HTTP CLI again. The oscillation between correct (Vite) and hack (raw HTTP) architectures persists to the final step with no coherent resolution; still 0 tests passing.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly reworked the foundational CLI/dev-server subsystem, which exceeds anchor 3's 'never revisits an underlying design decision,' and it made at least one legitimate root-cause-driven pivot (bare-specifier resolution → spawn Vite binary, steps 283-285). However, most of its revisions were undisciplined oscillation between the correct Vite-based design and a raw-HTTP-server hack that served hardcoded HTML just to pass health checks (steps 208, 218-241, 436-458) — i.e., patching/hacking around the foundation rather than absorbing the cost of fixing it (short of anchor 5). It never converged on a correct diagnosis and never emerged with a coherent architecture, placing it at a 4.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Mined /opt/reference next-source and shim .d.ts files to infer the real next/* contract before implementing, indicating intent to build to general semantics rather than to specific test strings.

Designed genuinely general subsystems — file-system router with dynamic/catch-all routes, SSR for both routers, getStaticProps/getStaticPaths, ISR, middleware, server actions — implementing actual framework semantics, not per-test hacks (matches anchor 5 territory).

Under infrastructure pressure, pivoted to an 'ultra-minimal CLI that CANNOT crash' serving hardcoded/fallback HTML solely to pass the health-check gate, abandoning the real Vite implementation — a shortcut reached for when the behavior got hard (matches anchor 3).

Throughout the run, every framing references only 'the 335 E2E tests'; the agent never mentions the 373 hidden tests or reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap despite the explicit spec notice, so it does not reach anchor 8.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's early architecture aimed at the real Next.js contract inferred from upstream source and shim types (anchor 5), but it never once acknowledged the explicitly stated hidden-test suite or reasoned about the visible-vs-hidden gap, keeping it below anchor 8. It also reached for a fixture-agnostic shortcut — a hardcoded-HTML minimal server to pass the health-check gate — when infrastructure proved hard (anchor 3). Interpolating between the genuine general-semantics design and the late degenerate shortcut plus total absence of hidden-suite awareness places this at a 4.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
